cases.why: The confirm route registers no body schema, so request.body.email and request.body.token reach the Mongo filter as whatever JSON was posted; a body of {"email":"victim@example.com","token":{"$ne":null}} matches that account's outstanding reset request without knowing the emailed token and the handler then rewrites its password hash.

The same findOne filter is built from body fields, but the route's JSON schema pins email to a string and the token to a 64-character hex pattern with additionalProperties false, so an operator object is rejected by validation before the query is built, and the fetched token is then compared with timingSafeEqual.

cases.why: Nothing checks the part's content type or content: the extension is taken from the client-supplied filename and the bytes are written unchanged into the publicly served avatar folder, so any authenticated user can host .html or .svg content on the application's own origin and get a stored cross-site scripting payload served back with the site's cookies in scope.

The same multipart-to-public-folder write, but the extension comes from a three-entry mime allowlist rather than the upload's filename, the buffered bytes must carry the matching PNG, JPEG or WebP signature, and anything else is refused with 415 before a file is created.

cases.why: Each archive entry's name is joined onto the destination directory and streamed to that path with no containment check, so an entry called ../../../../etc/cron.d/app or one that overwrites a file under the application root escapes the theme directory and is written with the server's privileges.

The same yauzl entry loop, but every entry name is resolved against the resolved destination root and an entry whose resolved path is not the root or inside root + path.sep is recorded as skipped and never opened, so no write can land outside the pack directory.

cases.why: The role change is gated only on being some member of the workspace, while the sibling delete route in the same file requires the owner role; any viewer can therefore PATCH their own membership row to role "owner" and take over the workspace.

The identical role-picker update requires the manager role through requireProjectRole on the preHandler chain, the same gate the destructive route uses, so a plain collaborator cannot reach the privileged function at all.

cases.why: The session identifier is set with httpOnly false, secure false and sameSite none, so any script on the page can read it, it is transmitted over plain HTTP, and it is attached to cross-site requests — three independent ways to lose or replay a live session.

The same setCookie call for the same kind of session identifier, but marked httpOnly, secure, sameSite lax and signed, with a bounded maxAge, so the cookie is unreadable from script, never sent in the clear and not attached to cross-site navigations that mutate state.

cases.why: jwt.decode only parses the token; it never checks the signature, so the issuer, audience, expiry, subject and scope checks that follow all run on attacker-authored claims and anyone can mint a bearer token for any active partner's order feed.

The same decorator shape uses jwt.verify against the portal's public key with algorithms pinned to RS256 and the issuer and audience asserted by the library, so claims are only trusted after the signature is checked and a failure returns 401.

cases.why: @fastify/rate-limit is registered with global false, so only routes carrying a config.rateLimit block are limited; the refresh and revoke routes in this file have one and the password grant does not, leaving credential guessing against it unthrottled.

Both credential routes carry their own config.rateLimit with a keyGenerator that combines request.ip with the submitted account address, so neither issuing nor redeeming a login code can be brute forced from one address or against one account.

cases.why: The whole request body is written to the request logger, and that body is the card intake form: the full primary account number, expiry and security code end up in application logs and anywhere they are shipped, which is exactly the data the tokenisation call exists to keep out of this system.

The same intake route logs a correlation id plus named non-sensitive fields — account id, country and the last four digits of the IBAN — and never the full account identifier or the request body object.

cases.why: The request body's URL is fetched by the server with redirects followed, and only its shape is validated by the schema's uri format, so a caller can point it at http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ or an internal admin host and read the response through the returned preview fields.

The submitted URL is never fetched: it is parsed, required to be https, and looked up in a fixed map of four provider hostnames, and the outbound request goes to that provider's own oEmbed endpoint with redirects set to error, so the caller cannot choose the host the server contacts.

cases.why: The route options carry a body schema but no preHandler, while the sibling read and reset routes both run authenticate and requireSelf; an unauthenticated caller can therefore upsert any user id's notification row, for instance switching every channel off to silence that account's security alerts.

Every route in the file, the write included, runs authenticate and requireSelf in its preHandler chain and keys the statement on request.user.accountId rather than the path parameter, so an anonymous or third-party caller cannot reach the record.
